faq.q: Is a 2000W induction enough for Indian cooking?
faq.a: Yes for daily Indian cooking -- chai, maggi, sabzi, dal-tadka, dosa, idli. Pressure-cooking dal takes about 12-15 minutes on a 2000W unit (vs 8-10 minutes on LPG). Below 1800W, induction struggles with cast-iron tawa cooking and pressure-cooking; you should not go below 1900W for Indian cooking.

faq.q: What is the difference between push-button and feather-touch panels?
faq.a: Push-button panels use physical switches that work reliably with wet or oily fingers. Feather-touch panels are capacitive -- they look sleeker and are easier to clean, but they often misfire when the cook's fingers are wet, oily, or covered in flour. In an Indian kitchen, push-button is the more practical choice for daily cooking.

faq.q: Do induction cooktops need special cookware?
faq.a: Yes. Induction works by magnetising the cookware base, so you need pots and pans with a ferromagnetic base -- stainless steel, cast iron, or induction-compatible non-stick. Aluminium, copper, and glass cookware will not work unless they have an induction-compatible base plate. Most induction-compatible cookware in India is labelled with a coil symbol on the box.

faq.q: Can I use a cast-iron tawa on induction?
faq.a: Yes, cast iron is ferromagnetic and works well on induction. The catch is that cast iron tawas are heavy (2-3 kg) and may scratch the glass top over time. Use a paper-thin layer of oil between the tawa and the glass, and lift (don't slide) the tawa when moving it. A well-seasoned cast-iron tawa on a 2000W induction is the closest you can get to traditional tava-cooked roti on a gas stove.

faq.q: Is induction cheaper to run than LPG?
faq.a: Per unit of heat, induction is roughly 80-85% efficient vs LPG at 35-40%. In practice, induction costs about Rs 4-6 per hour of cooking vs LPG at Rs 8-12 per hour (depending on cylinder subsidy state). For a household that does 2 hours of cooking per day, induction saves Rs 200-400 per month compared to a subsidized LPG cylinder. The catch: you need reliable electricity, which is not universal in India.

body:
What actually matters in an induction cooktop

An induction cooktop is one of the fastest-growing appliances in Indian kitchens, and the 2026 lineup has stratified enough that the wrong choice is usually picking a low-wattage unit or a feather-touch panel that fails on wet fingers. In 2026, the categories have stratified by wattage (1800W vs 2000W vs 2200W+), panel type (push-button vs feather-touch), and preset quality (Indian-tuned vs generic Chinese OEM).

The four things that actually move the needle on an Indian induction in 2026 are real wattage, panel type, Indian-tuned presets, and warranty length. Brand service network matters too, but the four major brands in this list (Prestige, Philips, Pigeon, iBELL) all have reachable service centres -- the gap is in panel type and preset tuning.

If you only buy one thing from this list: the Prestige PIC 20 2000-Watt Induction Cooktop. It has the real 2000W output, Indian auto-cook presets (roti, dosa, idli, curry, deep fry), push-button operation that survives oily fingers, and Prestige's widest service network in India.

Wattage: 2000W is the realistic floor for Indian cooking

An 1800W induction manages chai and basic sabzi fine, but it stalls on pressure-cooking dal and large-quantity tadka. The 2000W class is the realistic floor for a 4-5 person Indian household -- it handles pressure-cooking dal in 12-15 minutes, manages a full tawa of dosa batter, and doesn't trigger overheat protection mid-recipe. Below 1900W, you'll find induction tripping its thermal cutout during extended cooking sessions.

Panel type: push-button is more reliable than feather-touch

Push-button panels use physical switches that work reliably with wet, oily, or flour-covered fingers. Feather-touch panels are capacitive -- they look sleeker and are easier to wipe clean, but they misfire constantly when your fingers are wet after washing sabzi or oily after tempering masala. In an Indian kitchen, push-button is the practical choice. Feather-touch works fine in dry-lab or office-pantry environments, but for daily Indian cooking, push-button is the right answer.

Indian presets: Prestige and Philips tune for Indian food

Generic OEM induction presets are tuned for Chinese stir-fry and East Asian hot-pot cooking. Indian-tuned presets (Prestige PIC series, Philips Viva Collection) include specific modes for roti, dosa, idli, curry, deep fry, and pressure-cooking. These presets optimise the wattage curve for the specific task -- e.g. the dosa preset pulses the wattage to mimic the gas-stove tawa-cooking pattern. Generic OEM presets just step up to full power and let you manage temperature manually, which is harder for Indian recipes.

Warranty: 1-year is the minimum, 2-year is the real signal

Brand-published warranties range from 0 months (sub-Rs 1,500 marketplace listings) to 2 years (Philips Viva Collection). The standard 1-year warranty covers the glass top and the IGBT (the power component). Philips publishes 2 years on most Viva models, which is a real signal of build quality -- the brand is willing to back the unit for a second year of daily Indian cooking. Sub-Rs 1,500 listings usually publish 0-6 months and have no service network after the warranty expires.

1. Prestige PIC 20 2000-Watt Induction Cooktop

The Prestige PIC 20 is the default 2000W induction in India. The 2000W output handles pressure-cooking dal in 12-15 minutes and a full tawa of dosa batter without triggering thermal cutout. The Indian auto-cook presets (roti, dosa, idli, curry, deep fry) are tuned for daily Indian cooking, and the push-button panel survives oily fingers. Prestige's service network is widest across metros and tier-2 cities, with authorised centres in most state capitals.

Best for: anyone who wants the most balanced 2000W induction in India with Indian-tuned presets and a wide service network. Verify the exact model code (PIC 20, not the older PIC 16) on the listing -- Prestige has multiple variants and the older PIC 16 is still being sold at a lower price.

  • Indian auto-cook presets tuned for roti / dosa / idli
  • Push-button panel survives oily fingers
  • Prestige's service network is widest in India

✗ Trade-offs

  • 1-year warranty -- shorter than Philips Viva Collection (2 years)
  • Body is plastic at the edges -- minor wobble on uneven counters
  • No digital timer on the base model

Best for: buyers who prioritise raw wattage over Indian presets. Works well for pressure-cooking and deep-frying; less ideal for roti / dosa where Indian presets matter.

6. Sub-Rs 1,500 no-brand induction cooktops

Usually ₹2,400–₹2,900
Wattage1200-1600W
PanelFeather-touch
PresetsGeneric
Warranty0-6 months

The sub-Rs 1,500 induction listings promise 2000W with feather-touch panels and a 6-month warranty. The reality is 1200-1600W output, generic Chinese OEM presets, no IGBT protection, and no service network after the warranty expires. The glass tops scratch easily, the thermal cutout fails within 6-9 months, and the IGBT burns out on first pressure-cooking session in many cases.

We also recommend skipping any induction with 0-6 month warranty and no listed brand service centre in your city. The price difference between a sub-Rs 1,500 induction and the Pigeon Stovecraft (Rs 2,200-2,800) is Rs 700-1,300 -- which is the cost of replacing the cheap induction once. The Pigeon lasts 4-5 years; the cheap induction lasts 8-12 months.

  • Generic Chinese OEM presets

  • Glass top scratches easily
  • IGBT failure common within 6-9 months

The bottom line

Buy the Prestige PIC 20 if you want the most balanced 2000W induction in India with Indian-tuned presets and the widest service network. For a 2-year warranty and slightly higher wattage, the Philips Viva Collection HD4928/01 is the closest alternative. The Pigeon Stovecraft is the right pick on a tight budget around Rs 2,500.

For buyers who prioritise raw wattage over Indian presets, the iBELL Hold The World gives 2200W at a competitive price but with narrower service reach. The Prestige PIC 16.0+ is the budget pick under Rs 2,500 for light daily cooking -- but the 1900W output triggers thermal cutout on long pressure-cooking sessions. Whatever you pick, use ferromagnetic cookware (stainless steel, cast iron, induction-compatible non-stick) and avoid sliding cast-iron tawas across the glass top.
